dossier.topic: Snow-crystal dendrite tips: a speed-sharpness lock (V*R^2 = constant) plus side branches that sprout from a defect at a fixed distance behind the tip
dossier.summary: A dendrite grows by its tip, which is pushed forward by diffusion and capillary forces. Experiments on succinonitrile find that tip speed V and tip radius R obey V*R^2 = constant, so faster tips are sharper. Side branches do not appear at random: simulations and lab sequences show a defect forming at a characteristic distance behind the tip, which grows into a side branch. Snowflake arms follow six lattice directions, and side-branch length tracks how long that part of the front stayed growable.

facts.claim: Koss et al. (1999) report a kinetic selection rule for succinonitrile dendrite tips, V*R^2 = constant, where V is tip velocity and R is tip radius of curvature. They say it holds in microgravity, is nearly independent of gravity, and depends slightly on supercooling.
facts.source_title: Dendritic growth tip velocities and radii of curvature in microgravity

facts.claim: In microgravity, succinonitrile dendrite growth is diffusion-limited above about 0.4 K supercooling. On Earth, convection dominates dendritic growth below about 1.7 K supercooling.
facts.source_title: Dendritic growth tip velocities and radii of curvature in microgravity

facts.claim: In Gravner and Griffeath's 3D snow crystal simulation, a defect arises at a characteristic distance from the crystal tip, becomes more pronounced, and later gives rise to a side branch.
facts.source_title: Modeling Snow Crystal Growth III: three-dimensional snowfakes

facts.claim: The same simulation reproduces the crystal tip instability and the start of side branching studied in laboratory experiments, and the sequence matches the lab work of Gonda and Nakahara.
facts.source_title: Modeling Snow Crystal Growth III: three-dimensional snowfakes

facts.claim: Small bumps on a growing snow crystal develop into large branches, and bumps on those branches become side branches.
In Li and Schaposnik's model, the six main branches of a snow crystal grow along the lattice axes. Side-branch length indicates growth latency, the time a boundary cell spends before it freezes.
facts.source_title: Interface control and snow crystal growth

facts.claim: In Li and Schaposnik's model, growth direction takes six values measured from the horizontal axis: plus or minus 30, 90 and 150 degrees. Side branches are described as showing chaotic-dynamics features of complexity and unpredictability.
facts.source_title: Interface control and snow crystal growth

visualisable_mechanisms.name: V-R sharpness lock
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Tip speed and tip radius are tied by V*R^2 = constant, so a tip that speeds up becomes sharper and a slower tip blunts. The product stays fixed while the tip moves through changing supercooling.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: A needle tip whose point visibly thins as it accelerates and blunts as it slows, with the product of its speed and squared radius held on a fixed curve shown as a faint hyperbola.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: fixed-lag side-branch birth
visualisable_mechanisms.description: A defect appears at a characteristic distance behind the advancing tip, grows more pronounced, and then becomes a side branch. Each new branch is born at the same lag from the tip, so the spacing is set by the tip's motion.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: A moving tip leaves a trail of small bumps at a constant distance behind it; each bump swells over time into a short side arm with its own ridge.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: six-axis lattice arms
visualisable_mechanisms.description: The main arms grow along six lattice directions spaced 60 degrees apart. Side branches leave the main arms at fixed angles set by the lattice rather than at random.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Six straight arms radiating from a centre at 60 degree spacing, each with rows of short side arms at a fixed angle, so the figure has hexagonal symmetry as it grows.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: latency-length coupling
visualisable_mechanisms.description: A side branch's length reflects how long that stretch of the front stayed in the growable state before freezing. Longer latency gives longer branches, so the pattern records the timing of its own growth.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Side arms start at different times and freeze at different lengths: early-born arms stop short, late ones keep extending, showing a beginning, middle and end across the piece.

open_questions: Does the V*R^2 = constant rule measured in succinonitrile also hold for ice at snowflake growth conditions?
What sets the characteristic distance behind the tip where side-branch defects form in real ice crystals?
How closely does the latency-based model of Li and Schaposnik match the measured side-branch lengths in real snow crystals?

surprise.justification: A generalist expects a snowflake tip to be a free point set by the ice's six-fold symmetry alone. The data show tip speed and radius are locked by one rule, and side branches come from a defect at a fixed distance behind the tip rather than from random noise.

brief.title: Fixed-Lag Side Branches on a Dendrite Tip
brief.concept: A succinonitrile dendrite tip whose speed and radius are locked by V*R^2 = constant leaves side branches at a fixed lag behind itself, and the word defect is the row of letters where each branch is born.

mechanism_embodied.how_visualised: A clay-coloured tip advances outward from the centre and leaves the letters of the word defect at a constant lag behind it. Each letter swells into a branch-shaped side arm with its own ridge, so spacing is set by the tip's motion. Six main arms follow the lattice axes. Side arm length records how long that stretch of edge stayed growable, so early arms stop short and late arms keep extending. The tip visibly thins when it speeds up.

brief.discarded_obvious_idea: Obvious: a six-armed snowflake rotating on a gradient with random noise bumps along its edges. Rejected: random noise is on the slop list and hides the fixed-lag rule.
techniques: fixed-lag defect birth behind the tip
brief.motion_sound_plan: Mood: high tempo with five hard cuts at 5, 10, 11, 13 and 15 s over a dense field; warm-consonant palette of rose-clay and oxblood with six-fold mirrored symmetry; assertive framing, with the tip filling the frame at 2 s and a strong push or pull between beats. Experimental risk: signed-distance glyph growth. No audio (requires_audio is false), so no sound. Constraint is null.

storyboard.description: Sharp oxblood tip fills the centre of a rose-clay ground, thin and filling the frame. Behind it the word defect sits as a row of six small dots at equal spacing, not yet readable.

Tip advances outward. Each letter of defect swells through the glyph threshold into a branch-shaped arm, and six arms spread along the lattice axes. Camera pulls back to mid-scale with arms filling half the frame.
Hard cuts at 11 s and 13 s switch scale: the word branch is drawn letter by letter along each main arm as new side arms. Density peaks with all six arms full, oxblood on clay.

Pull back to the whole centred six-fold figure, mirrored. Early letters stop short while late ones keep extending, so arm lengths differ. The final frame shows the whole figure, unlike the close 2 s frame.

brief.memorable_moment: A row of letters behind a sharp tip, each letter swelling into a branch-shaped arm.
brief.self_declared_risk: The glyph threshold animation may read as random blobs if the lag between letters is not constant, and fwidth edges can alias at small sizes.
brief.liner_note: In 1999 Koss and colleagues reported that succinonitrile dendrite tips obey V*R^2 = constant, so faster tips are sharper. Gravner and Griffeath's three-dimensional snow crystal simulation finds a defect at a characteristic distance behind the tip, which later grows into a side branch. On screen the word defect sits as a row of letters behind a clay-coloured tip; each letter swells into a branch-shaped arm. Six main arms follow the lattice axes, and each side arm's length records how long its stretch of edge stayed growable.
